name: MSP430FR5720IRGER
title: 16-bit ultra-low-power FRAM microcontrollers, 4 KB to 16 KB, MSP430FR572x family
summary: The MSP430FR572x are 16-bit MSP430 microcontrollers that hold program and data in 4, 8 or 16 KB of ferroelectric RAM beside 1 KB of SRAM, running up to 8 MHz from 2 V to 3.6 V over -40°C to 85°C. Peripherals include a 10-bit 200 ksps ADC (on most parts), a 16-channel comparator, up to three eUSCI serial channels, five 16-bit timers, a calendar RTC, three-channel DMA, a 32-bit multiplier and CRC16. Seven low-power modes reach 6.3 µA in LPM3 and 0.32 µA in LPM4.5. The MSP430FR5720IRGER is the 4 KB part with ADC in the 24-pin 4 mm × 4 mm VQFN, on a 3000-piece reel.
key_figures: 16-bit MSP430, up to 8 MHz (no FRAM wait states)
4 KB / 1 KB (MSP430FR5720); 4, 8 or 16 KB FRAM across the family

operation.text: Ten devices share one die design and differ in FRAM size (16, 8 or 4 KB), in whether the 10-bit ADC is fitted, and in package. The odd-numbered parts (FR5721, 23, 25, 27, 29) come in the 40-pin RHA and 38-pin DA packages and carry two eUSCI_A channels, three Timer_B and up to 32 I/O; the even-numbered parts (FR5720, 22, 24, 26, 28) come in the 24-pin RGE and 28-pin PW packages with one eUSCI_A, one Timer_B and 17 or 21 I/O. FR5722, FR5723, FR5726 and FR5727 have no ADC. Every part has 1 KB SRAM, two Timer_A, one eUSCI_B and runs MCLK up to 8 MHz without FRAM wait states. The MSP430FR5720 has 4 KB FRAM, the ADC, and comes in RGE (17 I/O, ADC 6 external plus 2 internal channels, Comparator_D 10 channels) and PW (21 I/O, 8 plus 2 ADC channels, 12 comparator channels).

16-bit RISC core with sixteen registers: R0 is the program counter, R1 the stack pointer, R2 the status register, R3 the constant generator, and the other twelve are general purpose. A register-to-register operation takes one clock. The instruction set has the 51 original instructions in three formats plus extensions for the larger address range, seven source and four destination addressing modes, and works on bytes and words. Peripherals sit on the data, address and control buses and are reached by any instruction.

One active mode and seven low-power modes chosen in software. LPM0: CPU and MCLK off, ACLK on, SMCLK optional. LPM1 and LPM2: as LPM0 with the DCO also off. LPM3: only ACLK runs. LPM4: all clocks off. RAM and registers are kept in LPM0 to LPM4, and any interrupt wakes the part, runs its handler and can drop back to the same mode. LPM3.5 and LPM4.5 switch off the core regulator: data is lost but the I/O pad states are held; LPM3.5 keeps the RTC running and wakes on RST, a port pin or an RTC event, LPM4.5 wakes on RST or a port pin. Wake-up times are in the wake-up table.

The reset vector and all interrupt vectors live from 0FF80h to 0FFFFh; each holds the 16-bit address of its handler. Reset is at 0FFFEh with priority 63, the system NMI at 0FFFCh and the user NMI at 0FFFAh, then the maskable sources down to the RTC at 0FFCEh. SYSRSTIV, SYSSNIV and SYSUNIV report which event caused a reset or NMI.

Program, data and information memory are ferroelectric RAM. It is written through JTAG, Spy-Bi-Wire, the BSL, or by the CPU itself, with byte or word access, programmable automatic wait states, and ECC that corrects single-bit and detects double-bit errors. A word write takes 120 ns; endurance is 10^15 cycles; retention is 100 years at 25°C and 10 years at 85°C.

The MPU divides main FRAM into up to three segments. Access rights are set separately for each segment and for information memory, guarding against unintended CPU execution or writes, and access violations raise flags that can trigger an interrupt.
FRAM retention suffers at the high temperatures of reflow and hand soldering. Program the application only after the board is soldered; factory calibration data is built to survive J-STD-020 reflow.

A ROM bootloader loads FRAM or RAM over a UART on P2.0 (transmit) and P2.1 (receive), protected by a user password. It starts on a set sequence of edges on RST/NMI/SBWTDIO and TEST/SBWTCK; tools wait tSBW,En after the first rising edge on TEST before the falling edge.

Four-wire JTAG uses PJ.0 (TDO), PJ.1 (TDI/TCLK), PJ.2 (TMS) and PJ.3 (TCK), shared with general-purpose I/O; TEST/SBWTCK high hands these pins to JTAG, and RST/NMI/SBWTDIO is also wired to the tool. In JTAG mode TMS, TCK and TDI/TCLK get internal pullups. Two-wire Spy-Bi-Wire uses only TEST/SBWTCK as clock and RST/NMI/SBWTDIO as data. The embedded emulation module (S version) gives three memory-access breakpoints, one CPU-register-write breakpoint, combinable triggers, a cycle counter and per-module clock control; LPMx.5 can be debugged.

Up to four 8-bit ports plus port J. Every bit is set individually as input, output or interrupt, with a selectable pullup or pulldown. All port pins of P1 to P4 have edge-selectable interrupts and can wake the part from LPM3.5 and LPM4.5. Ports can be accessed by byte or in pairs as words.

Sources: XT1 in LF mode for a 32768 Hz watch crystal, XT1 in HF mode for a 4 to 24 MHz crystal (or either as a bypass clock input on XIN), the VLO (about 8.3 kHz), and the DCO with six factory-trimmed settings, which depend on the device; with DCORSEL = 0 the trimmed values are 5.37, 6.67 and 8 MHz, and DCORSEL = 1 with DCOFSELx = 3 gives 24 MHz. ACLK, MCLK (CPU) and SMCLK (peripherals) can each take any source. Every crystal source has fail-safe fault detection. MODOSC, about 5 MHz, clocks the ADC.

Keep the XT1 crystal close with short traces, surround XIN and XOUT with ground, keep other clocks and data lines away from them and run nothing under or beside those pins. Assembly residue and conformal coat must not add load or leakage between XIN and XOUT. Both crystal pins need external load capacitors; LF supports 6, 9 or 12 pF effective load, HF 14, 16 or 18 pF. The package adds about 2 pF per pin, and the board more, so check the result by measuring ACLK.

An internal LDO makes the 1.5 V core supply at VCORE, which needs a 470 nF capacitor (±20% or better) and at least ten times that capacitance on VCC; nothing else may load VCORE. Supervisors watch the supply (SVSH, trips falling at 1.88 V typical) and the core (SVSL), and a brownout circuit, always on and drawing no current, holds the part in reset during power-up and power-down. Power AVCC and DVCC from one source; they may differ by at most 0.3 V.
MPY32 multiplies 8-, 16-, 24- and 32-bit operands, signed or unsigned, with or without accumulation.
RTC_B is a calendar clock that knows month lengths and leap years, with alarms and offset calibration, and keeps running in LPM3.5. Its calibration clock can be brought out on RTCCLK (P1.0).
WDT_A resets the system if software fails to service it in time, or serves as an interval timer raising interrupts.
SYS handles power-on reset and power-up clear, NMI sources, the reset and NMI vector generators, bootloader entry, the device descriptors, and a JTAG mailbox for exchanging data with a debugger.

Three DMA channels move data between addresses without the CPU, for example ADC10_B results to RAM, so the CPU can stay asleep. Each channel picks one of 32 triggers, from timers, eUSCIs, the ADC, the multiplier, another channel, or the external DMAE0 pin.

eUSCI_A modules do UART (with automatic baud-rate detection), IrDA and 3- or 4-pin SPI; eUSCI_B does 3- or 4-pin SPI and I2C with multiple slave addresses. RHA and DA parts have eUSCI_A0, eUSCI_A1 and eUSCI_B0; RGE and PW parts have eUSCI_A0 and eUSCI_B0. The UART bit clock reaches 5 MHz, I2C SCL 400 kHz.

TA0 and TA1 (Timer_A) and TB0, TB1, TB2 (Timer_B) are 16-bit timers with three capture/compare registers each, for capture, PWM and interval timing, interrupting on overflow and on each register. RGE and PW parts have only TB0 of the Timer_B set. TBxOUTH pins on port J force a Timer_B's PWM outputs to high impedance.

10-bit SAR converter at up to 200 ksps, with sample-and-hold, internal reference, a result buffer and a window comparator whose high, low and in-window flags let it watch a signal without the CPU. Internal channels read the temperature sensor (channel 10) and AVCC/2 (channel 11). The external reference pins VeREF+ and VeREF- (P1.1, P1.0) need 10 µF and 100 nF of decoupling when used.

The on-chip sensor gives about 790 mV at 0°C and rises about 2.55 mV/°C, with a 51 kΩ source impedance needing 30 µs of sampling. Its offset varies a lot between parts, so calibrate it at one point; factory readings at 30°C and 85°C for each reference are stored in the device descriptor.

An analog comparator with up to 16 inputs, a 32-tap resistor-ladder reference and programmable hysteresis and output filter. It suits slope-type A/D conversion, battery supervision and watching outside analog signals. Its output CDOUT can be routed to pins and to timer capture inputs.
Hardware CRC on the CRC-CCITT polynomial produces a signature over a sequence of data words for integrity checks.
REF supplies 1.5 V, 2.0 V and 2.5 V references to the ADC and other analog blocks; the 2.0 V and 2.5 V settings need AVCC of at least 2.2 V and 2.7 V.

A tag-length-value table at 01A00h holds the device ID, revisions, die lot and position, test results, and per-chip ADC gain and offset, temperature-sensor readings and reference calibration values. Parts without the ADC report NA for the ADC calibration words.
On the RHA and RGE packages the exposed pad goes to VSS and is soldered to the board for heat and mechanical strength.
Device ESD ratings are ±1000 V HBM and ±250 V CDM; systems need their own ESD protection to keep overstress from damaging the part or disturbing memory contents.
